premises.text: Valuable web data is trapped in HTML pages without APIs, so only organizations that can hire developers can access it
premises.evidence_span: The majority of sites do not have an API, and creating one is complex

premises.text: A no-code data browser turns any web page into a live table or API in minutes by learning from example rows and columns
premises.evidence_span: turn any website. into a table of data or an API in a matter of minutes without writing code

premises.text: Created APIs can be combined so many sites stream into an application over a single API call
premises.evidence_span: Combining the API that I just created with other APIs is very easy

premises.text: A Data Factory Chrome extension gives anyone access to a growing library of ready-made APIs from pages they browse
premises.evidence_span: the Data Factory. The data factory is a chrome extension that will allow anybody to get access to our library of APIs

premises.text: There is always a free version of the product
premises.evidence_span: It's all free at the moment, and there will always be a free version

value.text: Anyone can easily access and use data from the web by turning sites into APIs
value.evidence_span: data on the web would be easily accessible to everyone

causal_links.evidence_span: Currently, this data is not available to everyone
with a couple of clicks, I've turned a web page into a table of data
instantly, the data is extracted from the site, formatted, and placed into a table
there will always be a free version

notes: User/API/page traction counts excluded as traction (§4.2); Red Cross and HP examples treated as applications of the same extraction mechanism (§4.1.2). Data Factory split as separately launched library/extension module. Vision that every website has an API treated as value framing, not premise (§4.1.4). Singleton D3/D4 retained. Anti-template: problem, extractor, library product, and free tier separately revisable.
